questions.question: An amoeba lives by itself in a pond and does every job of life as one cell. A muscle cell taken out of a person's arm and left on its own soon dies. Why can the muscle cell not live alone?
questions.answer: It has no blood to bring it food and oxygen
choices: It has no blood to bring it food and oxygen
It has no nucleus to direct its work
It has no mitochondria to release energy
It has no membrane to hold it together
questions.context: In a many-celled body each cell does its own job and relies on the others: blood, pumped by the heart, brings every muscle cell its food and oxygen. A muscle cell has a membrane, several nuclei and thousands of mitochondria, so it lacks none of those. An amoeba must find its food and take in its oxygen all by itself.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade units contrast one-celled organisms, which do every job themselves, with the specialised cells of a many-celled body, which cannot live on their own.

questions.question: Yeast lives wild in the soil and on the skins of fruit, in specks far too small to see. Under a microscope, each speck turns out to be a whole living thing made of a single cell. What is yeast?
choices: A one-celled fungus
A one-celled bacterium
A one-celled alga
A one-celled animal
questions.context: Yeast is a fungus, kin to mushrooms and moulds, but it lives as single cells. Unlike a bacterium, each yeast cell has a nucleus; unlike an alga, it cannot make its own food; and no animal is made of only one cell.
questions.grade_note: 6th grade sorts living things by one cell or many, and yeast is the standard example of a fungus that is a single cell.

questions.question: Some cells in the human body are up to a metre long, reaching from the lower back all the way down the leg to the foot. What job does one of these long cells do?
questions.answer: It carries signals along the leg
choices: It carries signals along the leg
It shortens to pull on the bones
It carries blood down to the foot
It holds the leg's bones together
questions.context: These are nerve cells, whose long, thin fibres carry signals between the spinal cord and the foot, so one cell can carry a signal the whole way. Muscle cells shorten to pull on bones, but even the longest is under a third of a metre; ligaments hold bones together, and blood flows in vessels built of many cells.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade lessons on many-celled organisms teach that specialised cells have shapes that suit their jobs, and the long nerve cell is the classic case.

questions.question: As a human red blood cell matures in the bone marrow, it pushes out its nucleus and most of its other parts. What does the cell gain by losing them?
choices: More room to carry oxygen
The power to divide faster
A longer life in the blood
A tougher, stiffer outer wall
questions.context: Its empty space fills with haemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen from the lungs to the body. With no nucleus, a red blood cell cannot divide and lives only about four months, and it has no wall at all: it is a soft disc that bends to squeeze through the tiniest blood vessels.
questions.grade_note: The red blood cell, built to carry oxygen, is one of the specialised cells a 6th grader meets, and its missing nucleus is the usual example of a cell shaped by its job.

questions.question: Euglena is a single cell with a red eyespot that swims through ponds with a whip-like tail. When a jar of pond water is set beside a bright window, the Euglena soon crowd to the side nearest the glass. What does this behaviour suggest about Euglena?
questions.answer: It makes its own food, as plants do
choices: It makes its own food, as plants do
It hunts by sight, as hawks do
It seeks warmth, as basking lizards do
It follows the others, as schooling fish do
questions.context: Euglena has green chloroplasts and makes its own food from light, so it swims to where the light is best; that makes it an autotroph, like a plant. Its eyespot only tells it which way the light lies and cannot see prey, and each cell steers toward the light by itself. In the dark, Euglena can take in food from the water instead.
questions.grade_note: 6th grade teaches that some single cells, such as one-celled algae, are autotrophs that make their own food, and Euglena swimming toward light is the textbook case.

questions.question: A Venus flytrap snaps two leaves shut on a fly in a fraction of a second, then digests it over the next several days. What does the plant mainly get from the flies it catches?
questions.answer: Nitrogen that is scarce in its soil
choices: Nitrogen that is scarce in its soil
Water that is scarce in its soil
Energy that its leaves cannot make
Oxygen that its leaves cannot take in
questions.context: A flytrap is still an autotroph: its green leaves make its food from sunlight, and it can live without catching a single fly. It grows in wet, boggy ground poor in nitrogen and phosphorus, and the flies make up for what its roots cannot find.
questions.grade_note: Autotrophs that make their own food are 6th-grade content, and a plant that eats insects yet still makes its own food tests what the word really means.

questions.question: Naturalists counted mushrooms and moulds as plants for centuries. Biologists now give fungi a kingdom of their own, and in one way fungi are more like animals than like plants. In what way?
questions.answer: They feed on food made by others
choices: They feed on food made by others
They move about from place to place
Their cells have no stiff outer walls
They sense the world through nerves
questions.context: Fungi and animals are both heterotrophs: neither can make its own food, so both take in food made by other living things, while plants and algae are autotrophs. Fungi stay put, have no nerves, and have stiff cell walls, made of chitin rather than the cellulose in plant walls.
questions.grade_note: 6th grade classes living things as autotrophs or heterotrophs and teaches that fungi are heterotrophs, not plants.

questions.question: A fuzzy mould spreads over a forgotten slice of bread, its fine threads growing down into the slice. How does the mould feed?
questions.answer: It digests the bread outside itself, then absorbs it
choices: It digests the bread outside itself, then absorbs it
It makes its own food from light, like a plant
It feeds on water it draws from the damp air
It lives on food stored in the spore it grew from
questions.context: The mould's threads pour digestive juices into the bread, break its starch into simpler food, and soak that food up. A fungus has no chlorophyll and cannot make food from light. Mould needs damp to grow, but water is not its food, and the tiny spore it grew from holds far too little to feed it.
questions.grade_note: That fungi cannot make their own food and instead absorb it, after breaking it down outside their bodies, is 6th-grade content on how fungi differ from plants.

questions.question: A paramecium is a single cell shaped like the sole of a slipper. It swims quickly through pond water, and when it bumps into something, it backs up and sets off another way. How does it move?
questions.answer: It beats thousands of tiny hairs
choices: It beats thousands of tiny hairs
It lashes one long, whip-like tail
It pushes out false feet and flows into them
It squirts jets of water out behind it
questions.context: A paramecium is covered in short hairs called cilia, which beat in waves like rows of oars; to back away, it reverses their beat. Euglena swims with one whip-like tail, called a flagellum, and an amoeba crawls by pushing out false feet.
questions.grade_note: The paramecium and its cilia are the standard 6th-grade example of a one-celled organism and how it moves.

questions.question: An amoeba is a single cell that creeps over the mud of a pond, feeding on even smaller living things such as bacteria. How does it take in a meal?
questions.answer: It surrounds the meal and closes it inside
choices: It surrounds the meal and closes it inside
It swallows the meal through a tiny mouth
It sweeps the meal in with a whip-like tail
It traps the meal in a sticky slime
questions.context: The amoeba pushes out arms of its cell, called pseudopods or false feet, around its prey until they meet and seal it inside a bubble, a food vacuole, where it is digested. An amoeba has no mouth and no tail.
questions.grade_note: How an amoeba surrounds and engulfs its food is the standard 6th-grade example of how a single cell eats.
